title: Understanding Artificial Intelligence in Everyday Terms 💡
intro: You do not need a computer science degree to understand artificial intelligence. This lesson explains what AI actually does, why it matters to everyday life, and how it quietly shapes the tools you already use.

sections.heading: 1. What is AI (and How is It Different from Regular Software)?

analogy.description: Regular software is like a pocket calculator, which follows the exact steps you give it and nothing more. AI is more like an apprentice chef, who studies many finished dishes and gradually learns what makes them taste good.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Most software follows fixed instructions: if you click here, it does this, and if you click there, it does that.

**Artificial Intelligence** works differently, because people do not write every rule by hand. Instead, the software studies a large collection of past examples, discovers the patterns inside them, and then makes its best guess about new situations. This is how your email application recognizes spam and how your navigation application predicts traffic before you leave home.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: The examples an AI studies so it can learn patterns.
A best guess based on patterns the AI has seen before.

diagram.caption: Regular software versus AI
diagram.alt: Two paths. Regular software takes data and human-written rules and produces an answer. AI takes data and example answers and produces its own rules.
diagram.content:
flowchart LR
    subgraph R["Regular software"]
        R1["Data + rules written by people"] --> R2["Answer"]
    end
    subgraph A["AI"]
        A1["Data + example answers"] --> A2["Rules learned from patterns"]
    end

sections.realWorld: Spam filters, map apps that predict traffic, and photo apps that group faces.

sections.heading: 2. Narrow AI vs. General AI: Cutting Through the Hype

analogy.metaphorName: The World-Class Espresso Machine vs. A Human Barista
analogy.description: An espresso machine can produce a perfect cup of coffee, but it cannot take your order, restock the napkins, or chat about the weather. That is Narrow AI. A human barista can handle all of those tasks without any special training.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
News stories often mix up two very different ideas, so it helps to separate them:

* **Narrow AI** is designed to do one job very well. Face unlock, fraud alerts, and voice typing are all examples, and **every AI system that exists today is Narrow AI.**
* **General AI** would be able to learn and reason about any subject the way a person can. It appears often in movies and marketing, but nobody has built it.

diagram.caption: Where Today's AI Actually Fits
diagram.content:
graph TD
    Tech["Artificial Intelligence Landscape"]
    Tech --> Practical["Narrow AI (100% of Today's Reality) ⚙️"]
    Tech --> Speculative["General AI / AGI (Theoretical Future) 🔭"]
    Practical --> App1["Smart Navigation & ETA Predictions"]
    Practical --> App2["Automated Translation (e.g. DeepL)"]
    Practical --> App3["Fraud Prevention in Banking"]
    Speculative --> Goal["Autonomous general problem solving (Unsolved)"]
diagram.alt: A tree. AI splits into Narrow AI, which is all of today's AI, with examples like navigation, translation and fraud detection, and General AI, which is a theoretical future goal.

sections.realWorld: Voice assistants and fraud alerts: each is good at one job only.

sections.heading: 3. Can Machines Truly Think? (The Turing Test)

analogy.description: Think of a support chat on a bank website, where you quietly wonder whether a person or a program is typing the replies. Alan Turing asked that same question back in 1950.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Alan Turing proposed a thought experiment called the **Imitation Game**. A person exchanges text messages with both a human and a computer, and if that person cannot reliably tell them apart, the computer has behaved intelligently.

Today's chat tools can sound remarkably natural. Even so, they work by predicting which word is likely to come next, and they do not understand language the way a person does.

interactiveWidget.title: 🔍 Quick Analysis: Bot or Human?
interactiveWidget.instruction: Examine this customer inquiry and decide which response was generated by an AI versus an empathetic human agent.

scenario.userPrompt: I just missed my connecting flight because of a maintenance delay, and my daughter's wedding is tomorrow afternoon. What can you do?
scenario.terminalA: I understand your flight was disrupted. Pursuant to Tariff Rule 240, you are eligible for the next available seat on Flight 412 departing tomorrow at 08:30 AM with a 2-hour layover.
scenario.terminalB: I am so sorry to hear that—what an incredibly stressful situation with your daughter's wedding on the line. Let me immediately check direct partner flights and emergency rebooking so we can get you there in time.
scenario.explanation: Terminal A mechanically cites tariff rules and procedures without contextual empathy. Terminal B demonstrates situational awareness and prioritized escalation, typical of experienced human support.

interactiveWidget.goal: Decide which reply came from an AI, then check your reasoning.
interactiveWidget.predictionPrompt: Before you choose: which reply do you think is automated, and what makes you say so?
hints: Look for emotion and specific detail.
Very polished, generic wording can be a sign.
interactiveWidget.successMessage: Good call. The point is not that bots always fail. It is that telling them apart takes care.

sections.realWorld: Customer-service chat windows where you wonder whether you are talking to a person.

sections.heading: 4. How Modern AI Actually Works: Rules vs. Machine Learning

analogy.metaphorName: The Corporate Employee Handbook vs. Mentorship
analogy.description: A 500-page policy manual tries to cover every situation in an office, yet real life is messy and unusual cases slip through the gaps. A new colleague, on the other hand, learns by watching experienced people and absorbing the unwritten habits of good work.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Computer scientists have followed two main paths toward building smart software:

1. **Rules first (top-down).** People write out detailed if-then rules, which works well for tax software or chess but fails for messy jobs such as driving through traffic.
2. **Examples first (bottom-up).** Engineers feed in millions of examples, and the computer finds patterns that no person could ever write down by hand. This approach is called **machine learning**.

diagram.caption: The Evolution from Traditional Logic to Machine Learning
diagram.content:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Trad ["Traditional Programming (Rule-Based)"]
        Input1["Data"] & Rules["Human Rules"] --> Engine1["Computer"] --> Out1["Output"]
    end
    subgraph ML ["Machine Learning (Data-Driven)"]
        Input2["Data"] & Out2["Desired Answers"] --> Engine2["Computer Training"] --> Model["Learned Model / Rules"]
    end
diagram.alt: Two flows. In traditional programming, data plus human rules go into a computer and produce output. In machine learning, data plus desired answers go into computer training and produce a learned model.

sections.realWorld: Tax software follows rules. Music apps learn your taste from what you play.

miniQuiz.question: Why did early rule-based AI struggle to recognize photos of cats or handwritten letters?
options: Computers in the 1980s did not have electricity
It is virtually impossible to write formal logical rules covering every possible angle, shadow, and posture
Cats are invisible to digital cameras
miniQuiz.explanation: Correct! Physical reality contains too many edge cases for handwritten 'if-then' statements. Machine learning solves this by learning visual patterns directly from data.

miniQuiz.question: Which statement accurately describes Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)?
options: It is currently operating in your smartphone's autocorrect feature
It is software that only works on Apple hardware
It is a theoretical system capable of human-level reasoning across all subjects, but does not currently exist
miniQuiz.explanation: Exactly right. Every AI application in commercial use today is Narrow AI designed for specific tasks.

teachBack.prompt: Explain AI to a colleague. Which sentence is the most accurate?
options: AI finds patterns in examples to make predictions.
AI is software that understands things like a person.
AI is any program with a lot of if-then rules.
teachBack.explanation: Today's AI finds patterns in data. It does not understand in a human way.
